claims.text: Serena is an open-source MCP toolkit from oraios/serena that provides symbol-level code retrieval, editing, and refactoring tools to MCP clients including Claude Code.
claims.notes: Executive summary; foundational framing of the tool.

claims.text: On a Debian-bookworm Python 3.11 devcontainer, the canonical install path for Serena is `uvx --from git+https://github.com/oraios/serena serena start-mcp-server`.
The uv tool itself is the only required prerequisite for Serena installation; uv is managed by uvx as a subcommand.
claims.notes: F-1 verbatim quote: 'Serena is managed by uv, and installing uv is the only required prerequisite.' (factual)

claims.text: An alternative install path is `uv tool install -p 3.13 serena-agent@latest --prerelease=allow` followed by invoking `serena` from PATH.

The base image `mcr.microsoft.com/devcontainers/python:1-3.11-bookworm` provides Python 3.11 but does not have uv pre-installed, so uv must be added via `pip install uv` or the official astral.sh/uv installer.
Upstream README's `uv tool install` example pins Python 3.13, but Python 3.11 is documented elsewhere as compatible (Itecs guide cites Python 3.10 or later).
Serena's docs warn that experimental Python 3.12+ may have LSP compatibility issues for some language backends.
Upstream explicitly warns not to install Serena via an MCP or plugin marketplace because those carry outdated commands.
Serena's default transport for MCP-client integration is stdio: the server is launched as a subprocess of the MCP client and communication is JSON-RPC over stdin/stdout.

Serena's HTTP mode is documented as a 'start the Serena MCP server yourself in HTTP mode and provide the client with the URL' pattern, where the operator runs Serena out-of-band and points the client at it.
SSE is referenced in Serena's changelog (HTTP/SSE mode bug fix in v1.2.0) but is not the documented default for client integrations.
For project-scoped `.mcp.json` always-on use, stdio is the correct transport for Serena.
If the design later wants to share one Serena instance across multiple containers or external clients, HTTP transport would become relevant.
For Claude Code project-scope, upstream recommends `claude mcp add serena -- serena start-mcp-server --context claude-code --project "$(pwd)"`.
The `--context claude-code` flag adapts Serena's tool descriptions and system prompts to Claude Code's conventions.
The `--project` flag binds the Serena server to a specific project root.

When using the uvx form without global install, the equivalent registration is `claude mcp add serena -- uvx --from git+https://github.com/oraios/serena serena start-mcp-server --context ide-assistant --project $(pwd)`.

Both registration forms produce a stdio-transport entry in `.mcp.json` of the standard shape: `{"command": "serena", "args": ["start-mcp-server", "--context", "claude-code", "--project", "<root>"]}` or with `"command": "uvx"` and appropriate args list.
Upstream notes that recent Claude Code / Opus model updates have 'drastically reduced adherence to instructions pertaining to Serena's tools' and recommends additional hooks.
Serena exposes roughly 20-25 MCP tools, grouped by function.

Serena's symbol-level retrieval tools include `find_symbol`, `get_symbols_overview` (file outline), `find_referencing_symbols`, `find_declaration`, `find_implementations`, and `diagnostics`/inspections.
Serena's symbolic editing tools include `replace_symbol_body`, `insert_after_symbol`, `insert_before_symbol`, and `safe_delete`.
Serena's refactoring tools include `rename` (symbol) and `propagate_deletions`.
Serena's basic non-symbolic utility tools include `search_for_pattern` (regex), `replace_content` (regex/literal), `list_dir`, `find_file`, `read_file`, and `execute_shell_command`.
Serena provides a memory-management subsystem of project-scoped notes the agent can write and recall, plus onboarding/project-init tools (`onboarding`, project-config commands).
JetBrains-only Serena tools — `move`, `inline`, `search in project dependencies`, `type hierarchy`, and breakpoint/variable debugging — are NOT exposed through MCP.

The exact MCP tool-id strings (consumed by Claude Code's `tools:` allowlist) are stable in snake_case form but should be confirmed at integration time by running `claude mcp list` against an installed Serena instance.

Serena's non-symbolic basic utilities (`search_for_pattern`, `read_file`, etc.) duplicate native Claude Code capabilities and contribute most of the context-window cost without unique value on a markdown-heavy repo.
Serena requires no API keys, OAuth tokens, or shared secrets for local stdio operation.

The only credential-shaped inputs to Serena are optional environment variables some language-server backends require (e.g., DOTNET_ROOT for F#); these are LSP backend prerequisites, not Serena authentication.
There is no Codespaces-secret surface area required for the Serena MCP server.
A separately paid JetBrains plugin for Serena exists with its own license; it is out of scope for MCP server integration.
The upstream oraios/serena repository follows semver release tags.
The latest stable Serena release tag at research time is v1.5.1, dated 2026-05-18 (onboarding-tool hotfix).
Serena v1.5.0 was released 2026-05-18 and added GDScript LSP via TCP.
Serena v1.3.0 was released 2026-05-11, adding Angular/HTML/SCSS/CSS/1C language servers, and contained a breaking config change replacing `base_modes` overrides in project.yml with `added_modes`.
Serena v1.2.0 was released 2026-04-27, adding Ada/SPARK, Svelte, Java-with-Lombok support, an HTTP/SSE bug fix, and a tool replacement of `ReplaceRegexTool` with `ReplaceContentTool`.
claims.notes: F-6 (factual + risk re tool-id breaking change).

claims.text: Serena v1.1.2 was released 2026-04-14.
The `uvx --from git+https://github.com/oraios/serena` form without a `@<tag>` suffix tracks `main` and is not suitable for production.
Serena version pinning should use either `uvx --from git+https://github.com/oraios/serena@v1.5.1 serena start-mcp-server` (tag-pinned) or `uv tool install serena-agent==1.5.1` (PyPI-package pinned).
Both v1.2.0 and v1.3.0 contain documented breaking changes; upgrading across either requires a config or tool-id review.
Recommended pin is v1.5.1 (or whichever is latest-stable at integration time) by git tag for transparency, since the tag appears in the `.mcp.json` arg list and is visible in code review.
Serena's value proposition is symbol-level code understanding built on Language Server Protocol backends per programming language.

Serena's symbol-level tools (`find_symbol`, `find_referencing_symbols`, `replace_symbol_body`, `type_hierarchy`, `find_implementations`, etc.) are operations over declarations, references, and types as defined by an LSP server for a source language.

Markdown is listed among Serena's 'supported languages' only in the broadest sense (the LSP ecosystem includes generic markdown servers for outline/link extraction), but upstream documentation provides no symbol-level capability listing for markdown.
Serena's marketed value is uniformly framed around code ("the IDE for your coding agent").

On a repo whose primary artifacts are markdown documents (specifications, KBs, PRDs, Plans, ADRs), Serena's symbol-level tools either return empty results or collapse to the basic-utility subset (`search_for_pattern`, `read_file`, `list_dir`, `find_file`).
Serena's basic-utility tools on markdown-dominant repos overlap heavily with Claude Code's native Read/Grep/Glob tools and provide no differentiation.
On a markdown-dominant repository, the always-on token cost of Serena's tool descriptions is paid every session for capabilities the agent rarely uses and that duplicate native tools.
claims.notes: F-7 conclusion (risk/analyst synthesis flagged in source as medium-high).

claims.text: If the repository contains a non-trivial code subdirectory (e.g., audit Python scripts, validator scripts), Serena's symbol-level tools apply to that subdirectory.
A server-wide always-on Serena registration pays full context cost even when only a small applicable code subtree benefits.

Option 1 for Serena integration is always-on with broad `tools:` exposure, paying full context cost (estimate: tool-description overhead for ~20 tools is meaningful) where most tools are unused most of the time on a markdown-dominant repo.

Option 2 for Serena integration is always-on with a narrowed `tools:` allowlist exposing only the basic-utility subset; this minimizes token-cost surface but eliminates Serena's differentiation versus Claude Code's native Read/Grep/Glob, making registration arguably redundant.

Option 3 for Serena integration is to drop Serena from the always-on set and keep it as on-demand, since discovery-codebase-researcher is already served by GitNexus (primary) and codebase-memory-mcp (fallback) per ADR-0018 and KB-codebase-research/SKILL.md.

Open question OQ-T1-1: the exact MCP wire-protocol tool-id strings (snake_case identifiers as they appear in `tools_list` over the MCP transport) are inferred from upstream documentation but not verified by direct invocation; resolution requires an integration smoke test.

Open question OQ-T1-2: whether Serena's `--context claude-code` system-prompt-override needs to be applied to the devcontainer's Claude Code launch, and whether the upstream warning about reduced instruction adherence with recent Opus models is load-bearing for adoption.

Open question OQ-T1-3: the estimated context-window cost (tokens) of Serena's tool descriptions when registered always-on cannot be answered by external research and must be measured at the Design stage against an installed instance.
mcp-openapi-schema is a Node.js (ESM) MCP server authored by Hannes Junnila.
claims.notes: Research note synthesizing primary sources (npm registry, GitHub repo). Treated as internal research output.

claims.text: mcp-openapi-schema loads a local OpenAPI 3.x file (JSON or YAML) and exposes 10 read-only schema-lookup tools to MCP clients.
mcp-openapi-schema is published on npm as mcp-openapi-schema@0.0.1 (MIT, single release dated 2025-03-13).
mcp-openapi-schema is run via `npx -y mcp-openapi-schema <path-to-spec>`.
Transport is stdio, confirmed in source via StdioServerTransport from @modelcontextprotocol/sdk.
mcp-openapi-schema has no authentication: the server reads a local spec file and emits schema fragments — no outbound HTTP, no credentials.
On the project's python:1-3.11-bookworm base image, nodejs + npm must be present; the devcontainer feature ghcr.io/devcontainers/features/node is the standard path.
Version-pinning recommendation: pin to mcp-openapi-schema@0.0.1 explicitly rather than relying on `npx -y` resolving 'latest'.
Future releases of mcp-openapi-schema may change tool shapes, and 0.0.1 is a pre-1.0 zero-version that could undergo breaking churn.
The npm package mcp-openapi-schema is at version 0.0.1.
The npm package mcp-openapi-schema is MIT-licensed.
The npm package mcp-openapi-schema was first and only published on 2025-03-13.
mcp-openapi-schema dependencies are @apidevtools/swagger-parser ^10.1.1, @modelcontextprotocol/sdk ^1.7.0, js-yaml ^4.1.0, zod ^3.24.2.
The mcp-openapi-schema entry point is index.mjs; bin exposes a mcp-openapi-schema command.
Package description per package.json: 'A Model Context Protocol server that exposes OpenAPI schema information to Large Language Models'.
claims.notes: Verbatim quote from package.json as cited in research note.

claims.text: mcp-openapi-schema is a pre-1.0 version (0.0.1) with no release history.
The mcp-openapi-schema package has been static since March 2025 (~14 months as of research date).
The mcp-openapi-schema index.mjs source imports StdioServerTransport from @modelcontextprotocol/sdk/server/stdio.js and connects the server to it as the sole transport.
mcp-openapi-schema has no HTTP/SSE transport option.
An HTTP wrapper for mcp-openapi-schema would have to be built externally.
For a local devcontainer scenario, stdio is the standard and recommended MCP transport.
mcp-openapi-schema exposes 10 tools, all read-only against the loaded OpenAPI spec, with no mutation/write operations.
Tool list-endpoints lists all API paths and HTTP methods with summaries.
Tool get-endpoint returns full detail for one endpoint (parameters, responses).
Tool get-request-body returns the request body schema for an endpoint/method.
Tool get-response-schema returns the response schema for an endpoint/method/status.
Tool get-path-parameters returns parameters for a given path.
Tool list-components lists components/* (schemas, responses, parameters, etc.).
Tool get-component fetches one component definition.
Tool list-security-schemes lists the spec's declared security schemes.
Tool get-examples returns examples attached to components or endpoints.
Tool search-schema searches across paths, operations, and schemas.
claims.notes: Verbatim README fragment quoted in source.

claims.text: mcp-openapi-schema output is rendered as YAML for LLM consumption.
mcp-openapi-schema tool names use hyphenated kebab-case (e.g., list-endpoints, not listEndpoints).
Installation of mcp-openapi-schema requires Node.js + npm.
The standard invocation for mcp-openapi-schema is `npx -y mcp-openapi-schema /absolute/path/to/openapi.yaml`.
For Claude Code CLI registration of mcp-openapi-schema: `claude mcp add openapi-schema npx -y mcp-openapi-schema`.
Declarative config for mcp-openapi-schema in Claude Desktop / .mcp.json uses command 'npx' with args ['-y', 'mcp-openapi-schema', '/ABSOLUTE/PATH/TO/openapi.yaml'] under mcpServers.openapi-schema.
The project's base image (mcr.microsoft.com/devcontainers/python:1-3.11-bookworm) does not include Node.js by default.

claims.text: The devcontainer must add ghcr.io/devcontainers/features/node:1 (or install Node via apt/nodesource) to make npx available.
The mcp-openapi-schema package.json does not declare an engines.node constraint.
The @modelcontextprotocol/sdk@^1.7.0 requires Node >= 18 in practice.
Recommendation: use Node 20 LTS via the devcontainer feature.
The mcp-openapi-schema server reads a local OpenAPI file path passed as a CLI argument and exposes schema fragments to the MCP client over stdio.
There is no outbound HTTP, no API-key handling, and no auth flow in mcp-openapi-schema.
The list-security-schemes tool reports the security schemes declared in the spec — it does not authenticate against the API the spec describes.
Playbooks listing states 'No external API credentials needed' regarding mcp-openapi-schema.
claims.notes: Verbatim short quote from Playbooks listing per source.

claims.text: If the loaded spec contains sensitive endpoint paths or examples (real customer IDs, internal-only URLs), those become visible to the LLM via the mcp-openapi-schema server.
Only one version (0.0.1) of mcp-openapi-schema has been published.
`npx -y mcp-openapi-schema` will resolve to whatever is 'latest' at the moment of invocation.
For reproducible devcontainer provisioning, pin the mcp-openapi-schema version explicitly: `npx -y mcp-openapi-schema@0.0.1 …`.
The pre-1.0 version number of mcp-openapi-schema signals that breaking changes may land without semver protection in any future release.
claims.notes: Source rates F-6 medium-confidence (pinning recommendation is researcher synthesis).

claims.text: If mcp-openapi-schema remains unmaintained, a pinned 0.0.1 will eventually develop CVE exposure via its transitive deps (notably js-yaml, swagger-parser).
The devcontainer should treat MCP server packages as periodic-review supply-chain dependencies.
Stdio is the canonical local-devcontainer MCP transport — no HTTP listener, no port to manage, no auth surface.
The mcp-openapi-schema tool surface is entirely schema-inspection; there is no attack path where an LLM call mutates a remote system through this server.
No secret needs to live in the devcontainer image or in .mcp.json for the mcp-openapi-schema server.
Adding the Node devcontainer feature is a one-line addition but is a real dependency that must be tracked.
The dominant risk for mcp-openapi-schema is project maintenance: a single 0.0.1 release from March 2025 with no follow-ups.
Mitigation option: pin @0.0.1 and accept that a periodic supply-chain review is required.
Mitigation option: fork mcp-openapi-schema to an org-owned mirror if longer-term reliance is anticipated.
The feature design should call out the maintenance risk explicitly in the ADR that selects this server.
Pre-1.0 versions provide no semver guarantees, so unpinned use is unsafe for a reproducible devcontainer.

The install command `npx -y mcp-openapi-schema@0.0.1 <path>` works on Debian-bookworm + Node/Python toolchain once ghcr.io/devcontainers/features/node:1 is added; Python toolchain not required (Node-only).

The mcp-openapi-schema server takes a single file path as a CLI argument; to expose multiple specs simultaneously, multiple server instances must be registered (each as a separate MCP server with a distinct name).
@apidevtools/swagger-parser parses the entire OpenAPI spec into memory; very large specs (multi-MB) could affect MCP server startup latency.

claims.notes: F1 primary claim; quoted from go.mod and main.go inspection.

claims.text: The actionlint Go-library dependency in actionlint-mcp is statically resolved at build time, not at runtime.
actionlint-mcp's go.mod lists github.com/rhysd/actionlint v1.7.7 on the default branch main as of 2026-05-23.
actionlint-mcp's main.go contains import "github.com/rhysd/actionlint" and uses actionlint.NewLinter(io.Discard, opts) followed by linter.Lint(filePath, content, nil).
Consumers of actionlint-mcp cannot independently upgrade the embedded actionlint version without rebuilding the MCP.

The actionlint-mcp README advertises the install command: curl -sSfL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hongkongkiwi/actionlint-mcp/main/install.sh | sudo sh.
The install.sh script downloads from https://github.com/hongkongkiwi/actionlint-mcp/releases/download/$VERSION/$FILENAME, defaulting $VERSION to "latest" via the GitHub releases API.
The hongkongkiwi/actionlint-mcp repository's Releases page currently lists no releases ("There aren't any releases here") as of 2026-05-23, so install.sh has no artifacts to download.

claims.text: Among the four install methods the actionlint-mcp README lists (install script, prebuilt binaries, go install, Docker), only go install github.com/hongkongkiwi/actionlint-mcp@latest does not depend on release assets.

The target devcontainer base image mcr.microsoft.com/devcontainers/python:1-3.11-bookworm ships no Go toolchain.

The latest stable rhysd/actionlint release as of 2026-03-30 is v1.7.12.
The standalone actionlint CLI binary is optional for actionlint-mcp's operation.
Installing the standalone actionlint CLI alongside actionlint-mcp introduces drift between the version statically linked into the MCP and the version installed as CLI.
actionlint-mcp runs as a stdio MCP server invoked directly by the client (e.g., Claude Desktop launches /usr/local/bin/actionlint-mcp with no transport flags).
actionlint-mcp exposes exactly two tools: lint_workflow and check_all_workflows.
The lint_workflow tool takes parameters file_path or content and lints a single workflow file or inline YAML.

claims.text: The compiled binary path is configured as a stdio MCP server pointing at the local binary path.
The GitHub README documents `go install github.com/hashicorp/terraform-mcp-server/cmd/terraform-mcp-server@latest` as an install option.
The `go install` install path requires the Go toolchain to be present.
An official image `hashicorp/terraform-mcp-server` is published on Docker Hub.
The Docker image is runnable in stdio mode via `docker run -i --rm hashicorp/terraform-mcp-server:0.5.2`.
Running the Docker image requires a Docker daemon, which is incompatible with the no-DinD base-image constraint.
The terraform-mcp-server supports two transports: stdio (default) and streamable-HTTP.
HTTP transport mode is enabled via `TRANSPORT_MODE=streamable-http` with `TRANSPORT_HOST` and `TRANSPORT_PORT`.
HTTP mode introduces a listening port and CORS/auth surface via `MCP_ALLOWED_ORIGINS` and `MCP_RATE_LIMIT_*`.
Tools are partitioned into toolsets selectable via `--toolsets`: `registry`, `registry-private`, and `terraform`.
The `registry` toolset provides anonymous public-registry access.
The `registry-private` toolset (private modules/providers) requires HCP/TFE authentication.
The `terraform` toolset covers HCP Terraform / Enterprise workspace, run, variable, policy, and stacks operations.

Registry toolset tools include `search_providers`, `get_provider_details`, `get_latest_provider_version`, `search_modules`, `get_module_details`, `get_latest_module_version`, `search_policies`, and `get_policy_details`.

Terraform toolset tools include `list_terraform_orgs`, `list_workspaces`, `get_workspace_details`, `create_workspace`, `update_workspace`, `delete_workspace_safely`, `list_runs`, `get_run_details`, `create_run`, `action_run`, `get_plan_json_output`, `get_plan_details`, `get_plan_logs`, `get_apply_details`, `get_apply_logs`, `list_variable_sets`, `create_variable_set`, `attach_variable_set_to_workspaces`, `list_workspace_variables`, `list_stacks`, `get_stack_details`, and `attach_policy_set_to_workspace`.
Stacks support was added to terraform-mcp-server in the 0.5.x line.
Some tools have destructive effects, including `delete_workspace_safely` and the `create_run` then `action_run` sequence.
Public Terraform Registry operations (provider docs, module discovery, Sentinel policies in the public registry) require no authentication.
HCP Terraform or Terraform Enterprise operations require `TFE_TOKEN`.
`TFE_ADDRESS` defaults to `https://app.terraform.io`.
`TFE_SKIP_TLS_VERIFY` is an additional environment variable knob for HCP/Enterprise operations.
Shipping with `--toolsets registry` and no `TFE_TOKEN` provides a read-only profile that avoids any secret-handling requirement.
Each terraform-mcp-server release publishes signed checksum files: `terraform-mcp-server_<VER>_SHA256SUMS`, `terraform-mcp-server_<VER>_SHA256SUMS.sig`, and a key-ID-suffixed signature file.
Recent terraform-mcp-server releases are: 0.5.2 (Apr 28), 0.5.1 (Apr 7), 0.5.0 (Apr 1), 0.4.0 (Jan 22), plus the 0.3.x line.
terraform-mcp-server is pre-1.0 and expected to undergo periodic breaking changes; pin to exact patch and re-verify on bump.

The Docker image install path requires a Docker daemon and violates the no-DinD constraint.

The default configuration for this feature uses stdio transport, `--toolsets registry` for an anonymous read-only profile, and leaves `TFE_TOKEN` unset.
If the team later wants HCP Terraform tooling, the `TFE_TOKEN` flag can be added without re-provisioning the binary.

Context7 is Upstash's library-documentation-lookup MCP server.

claims.text: Context7 is distributed as a vendor-hosted remote HTTP endpoint at https://mcp.context7.com/mcp.
Context7 is distributed as a local stdio server published as the npm package @upstash/context7-mcp.
The same --api-key (or CONTEXT7_API_KEY env var) authenticates both the remote HTTP and local stdio transports.
A Context7 account/API key is recommended for usable rate limits but is not strictly required for anonymous low-volume probing.

For project-scoped always-on use under the feature's Codespaces baseline, the recommended transport is remote HTTP to https://mcp.context7.com/mcp with the API key supplied as a request header sourced from the CONTEXT7_API_KEY Codespaces secret.

claims.text: Using the remote HTTP endpoint avoids version drift on a vendor-controlled service that re-indexes upstream library docs constantly.
Using the remote HTTP endpoint eliminates a Node process from the always-on session.
The local stdio install command npx -y @upstash/context7-mcp remains a documented fallback if remote egress is blocked.
The Context7 CLI exposes a --transport flag (stdio vs http) and a --port flag (default 3000) for the local-http case.
